lesson.title: The Stop Shift (D → T)
lesson.subtitle: From day to Tag, door to Tür, drink to trinken, and dream to Traum

hook.title: The Consonant Domino
hook.content: Linguistic shifts happen in chains. When ancient Germanic 'th' hardened into 'd' (think ↔ denken), the existing Germanic 'd' had to move forward to prevent words from colliding. It hardened from a voiced stop into a crisp voiceless stop: 't'. This explains why English 'd' consistently mirrors German 't'.

footnotes.title: Devoicing of Alveolar Stops
footnotes.content: Voiced alveolar stop [d] hardened into voiceless alveolar stop [t] during the Second Germanic Sound Shift.

pattern.title: Initial, Medial, and Final D becomes T
pattern.content: Day becomes Tag. Door becomes Tür. Drink becomes trinken. Dream becomes Traum. Table becomes Tisch (via Latin discus ↔ dish ↔ Tisch: a table was historically the 'dish-board'!). In the middle and end of words, the rule holds firm: yard/garden becomes Garten, cold becomes kalt, good becomes gut, and word becomes Wort. Daughter becomes Tochter—a double shift pairing initial D → T with guttural GH → CH!

footnotes.title: Dish ↔ Tisch
footnotes.content: Both languages borrowed Latin discus. English softened the end into 'dish' and kept initial d; German hardened initial d to t and palatalized the sibilant into Tisch.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the German verb for 'to drink' using the D → T shift (drink + en):
exercises.affirmation: You hardened the d into t and hung the -en — drink is trinken now.
exercises.explanation: Initial D hardens to T: stem 'trink-' + infinitive ending '-en' = trinken.

exercises.prompt: Match each English D word with its hardened German T twin:
exercises.affirmation: Four d-words hardened on sight — Tag, Tür, Tochter, Traum: the domino, live.
exercises.explanation: Where English preserved Germanic D, High German hardened it into T.

exercises.prompt: Which two sound shifts connect English 'deep' to German 'tief'?
exercises.affirmation: You ran two shifts in one word — d to t, then p to f: deep became tief.
exercises.explanation: Initial D hardened to T (deep → teep), and post-vocalic P shifted to F (teep → tief).

exercises.prompt: Apply the D → T shift: English 'cold' → German adjective:
exercises.affirmation: You hardened the final d to t — cold ends crisp, the way German likes it.
exercises.explanation: Final D hardens to T, with vowel alignment: cold ↔ kalt.

exercises.idea: you walk into a café at noon: you greet with good day, then say what you'll drink — cold water
cues: Greet first: Guten Tag — both words run D → T
What? → kaltes Wasser: cold → kalt, with the -es ending of neuter Wasser
exercises.target_answer: Guten Tag ich trinke kaltes Wasser
exercises.meaning: Good day! I drink cold water

vocab_hints.note: D → T shift in both words: good ↔ gut, day ↔ Tag

exercises.explanation: Greeting formula, then subject + verb in position 2 + object — a whole little scene, built from a thought.

summary.outcome: Use a few d/t cognates in a greeting and a simple present-tense sentence.

use_example.german: Guten Tag! Ich trinke kaltes Wasser.
use_example.english: Good day! I drink cold water.

summary.takeaway: English 'd' systematically corresponds to German 't' at the beginning, middle, and end of words.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the double-shift detectives — deep becomes tief and daughter becomes Tochter: two rules at once.

twist.prompt: Same water, shared: I drink cold water becomes we drink cold water. (The verb ending goes back to the stem.)
twist.explanation: ich trinke → wir trinken: the ending returns to the bare stem's -en, the one the dictionary form wears. And kaltes Wasser doesn't budge.

tag.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and y → g.

tür.etymology_derivation: d → t with vowel mutation to ü.

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

garten.context_translation: The children play in the garden.

tochter.context_phrase: Meine Tochter lernt in der Schule.
tochter.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and gh → ch.

wort.etymology_derivation: Final d → t. Plural: Wörter / Worte.

tisch.context_phrase: Der Teller steht auf dem Tisch.
tisch.context_translation: The plate stands on the table.
tisch.etymology_derivation: Latin discus → Old English disc (dish/desk) → Old High German tisc (tisch, with d → t).

tief.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and p → f.

taube.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and v → b.

toll.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *dulaz 'foolish, dazed' — the same word as English dull, which etymonline lists beside German toll; German hardened d to t and the sense flipped from mad to great. [wiktionary] [etymonline]

abends.context_translation: In the evenings I read a book.
abends.etymology_derivation: Abend + adverbial -s, from an old adverbial genitive — the twin formation of the English adverb evenings. [wiktionary]

hochzeit.etymology_derivation: hoch + Zeit, literally high time or high festival (Old High German hohun giziti); the Zeit element is the twin of English tide, as documented in the dictionary Zeit row. [wiktionary]

not.context_phrase: Er half mir in meiner Not.
not.context_translation: He helped me in my time of need.
not.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *naudi; the page lists English need as a direct cognate, with the d of need hardening to t in Not. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
